newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZDB gains reversal of U.S. decision on trust laws.
newsitem.headline: NZDB gains reversal of U.S. decision on trust laws.

text.p: The New Zealand Dairy Board said on Friday it had fended off charges in a U.S. District Court which threatened to show that U.S. courts had jurisdiction over how New Zealand producer boards market their products in the United States.
Dairy Board chairman Sir Dryden Spring said the court had reversed its ruling of last year that the board had a case to answer under U.S. anti-trust law, the New Zealand Press Association reported.
The decision had far-reaching implications for both the dairy industry and New Zealand exporters generally, Spring said in a statement.

The U.S. court now held that the Dairy Board Act required the board to decline any application to export to the U.S. market, which meant the board was exempted from compliance with U.S. anti-trust law, he said.

A New York district court judge last year refused to strike out charges and counter-charges involving a board subsidiary and an American company, the most significant of which had serious implications for single-desk New Zealand food exporters.

The dispute is reported to have begun in 1993, when American distribution company Trugman-Nash and Trio Cheese Imports received but did not pay for about NZ$2.98 million of cheese from Dairy Board subsidiary Western Dairy Products.
Trugman-Nash claimed the board and its companies deliberately delayed delivery to force a higher price, and claimed the board's export monopoly violated the Sherman (anti-trust) Act.

Trugman-Nash said New Zealand's then 15 dairy cooperatives had formed a cartel in violation of U.S. laws, but argued there was nothing in Dairy Board legislation that compelled violation of anti-trust laws.

Counsel for the Dairy Board argued that U.S. anti-trust laws could not apply because it was compelled by the New Zealand government to sell on a single-desk basis, and pleaded "comity" -- one nation deferring to the larger involvement or concerns of another on a particular matter.

U.S. district court judge Charles Haight heard all these charges in October last year, and effectively ruled that the U.S. courts had jurisdiction over how the Dairy Board markets its products there. He refused to strike out any of the actions.

If this ruling had been confirmed, the result of the subsequent trial could mean trouble for not only the Dairy Board but New Zealand's other single-desk exporters, the Kiwifruit Marketing Board and the Apple and Pear Marketing Board.
But Spring said on Friday the reversal of the judge's ruling was a welcome recognition of New Zealand law intended to maximise export returns to the New Zealand dairy farmer.
